title: The Last Message to Daruka
story:
The hunter who had shot the arrow could not stop trembling. His name was Jara, and he hunted the forests near Prabhasa. His arrow had struck the foot of a man resting in the grass — and the man was Krishna, the Lord of the universe, who had come down from heaven to live among men. The hour the gods had been promised was upon him.

Krishna looked at the hunter, and his voice was gentle. "Do not be afraid," he said. "Rise. This was my own doing." Then he gave the hunter the last thing he could have expected to hear: "Go, with my leave, to the world of the good." The man whose arrow had brought about his death was not cursed but blessed; the arrow had only done what Krishna himself had arranged. Jara rose, went his way, and was saved.

Then his charioteer Daruka came. Krishna had sent him away, and Daruka, searching for his master's path, had found him at last — at the foot of an ashvattha tree, the great pipal, ringed by the divine weapons of Vishnu, for Krishna and Vishnu are one, which stood blazing guard over their lord. Daruka leapt from the chariot and fell at Krishna's feet, his heart flooding with love, his eyes full of tears.

"Master," he wept, "your lotus feet are hidden from my sight. It is as though my eyes have failed and I have fallen into darkness."

Even as he spoke, the chariot — the one that bore the image of Garuda, the great eagle of heaven, on its banner, the one that had carried Krishna through every war — rose into the air, and the divine weapons rose with it, following their master out of this world.

Krishna looked at his charioteer with the old fondness and gave him the last message he would ever send. "Go to Dwaraka, Daruka," he said. "Tell my kinsmen of their destruction — they have slain one another. Tell them Balarama is gone, and tell them the state I am in. Do not stay in Dwaraka, you or your relatives. Take all your possessions, every one of you, and with Arjuna's help lead the people to Indraprastha. The sea will soon flood the city I have left."

It was a message for a whole city: a people to be moved, a flood to be outrun, a road pointed out to safety. The kinsmen were the Yadavas, his own clan; Balarama was his elder brother; and Arjuna, the Pandava prince who had been his closest friend among men, would come with his chariot to lead the survivors east, to Indraprastha, the city of the Pandavas.

And then, for the charioteer himself, one final word of counsel. "But you, Daruka," Krishna said, "hold to the dharma I have taught you — the right way of living. Be firm in knowledge. Let the pairs of opposites — pleasure and pain, gain and loss — come and go without shaking you; look on all things as one."

Daruka circled his master, bowed again and again, and went on his way to Dwaraka, carrying the last words of Krishna in his heart. Behind him, beneath the pipal tree, the stillest figure in the world remained, guarded by weapons that were no longer there. The last message had been sent; there remained only the last departure — the one that no messenger could carry and no friend could delay.
reflection: The last message is not about Krishna at all but about everyone he is leaving: a people who must move before the sea comes, a hunter forgiven for what he could not know, a charioteer told how to live after his master is gone. Even in leaving, he is arranging the world's safety — and his final counsel to Daruka, to stand firm in knowledge and indifferent to loss and gain, is his whole teaching compressed into a goodbye.
next_story_tease: The last message sent, only Krishna's own departure remained.
